The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: Parametrize the oriented edge $[x_i,x_j]$ by $x(t)=(1-t)x_i+tx_j$, $0\le t\le1$. Along it, $\lambda_i=1-t$, $\lambda_j=t$, so $\nabla\lambda_j\cdot x'(t)=1$ and $\nabla\lambda_i\cdot x'(t)=-1$. Therefore $\phi_{ij}(x(t))\cdot x'(t)=(1-t)-t(-1)=1$, and $\ell_{ij}(\phi_{ij})=1$.

Let $[x_r,x_s]$ be a different edge. If it shares no endpoint with $[x_i,x_j]$, then both $\lambda_i$ and $\lambda_j$ vanish identically along $[x_r,x_s]$, so its circulation is zero. If it shares $x_i$, then $\lambda_j$ vanishes identically along that edge and its directional derivative also vanishes; the remaining term $-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ is zero. The case sharing $x_j$ is symmetric. Thus $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=0$ whenever $(r,s)\ne(i,j)$.

Each $\phi_{ij}$ is affine in $x$. Its linear part is the skew-symmetric map $x\mapsto(
abla\lambda_j\cdot x)
abla\lambda_i-(
abla\lambda_i\cdot x)
abla\lambda_j$, hence equals $b_{ij}	imes x$ for a unique $b_{ij}\in\mathbb R^3$; its constant part is a vector $a_{ij}$. The space $\{a+b	imes x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$ has dimension six: if $a+b	imes x=0$ on the open tetrahedron, subtracting the values at two points shows $b	imes y=0$ for every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, so $b=0$ and then $a=0$. The six functions are linearly independent because their circulation matrix is the identity by steps 1.1–1.2. They therefore form a basis of this six-dimensional space, and the six moments are unisolvent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open and set
$$H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)}^{\,H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)},$$
where the norm is that of [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. This is the closure-defined zero-tangential subspace used on this page. Identifying this closure with the full kernel of a particular boundary trace map is not part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Orient every top-dimensional cell of a matching simplicial mesh by the
ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced
boundary convention of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. In the sum
of the oriented boundaries of all top-dimensional cells, every interior
facet occurs twice with opposite signs; every boundary facet occurs once.

If $K\subseteq U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq U$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Suppose
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact
set $K_0\subset\Omega$. Let $E_0u$ denote the extension of a representative of
$u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$, and for $|\alpha|\le k$ let
$E_0(D^\alpha u)$ denote the extension by zero of the corresponding
derivative representative. Then
$$E_0u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad D^\alpha(E_0u)=E_0(D^\alpha u)\quad\text{almost everywhere, }|\alpha|\le k,$$
and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0(D^\alpha u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. The case
$k=0$ is included, and complex scalars are handled by the same bilinear
pairing.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. Then the six edge circulations $\ell_{rs}(v)=\int_{[x_r,x_s]}v\cdot t_{rs}\,ds$ satisfy $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=\delta_{(r,s),(i,j)}$. $$\int_{\Delta^k}d\eta=\sum_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\int_{\Delta^{k-1}}\delta_i^*\eta,$$
where the integrals and ordered face maps use the standard affine-simplex conventions. No Stokes theorem for manifolds with corners is assumed.

$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$

the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

ambient orientation of $\mathbb R^d$, and orient each facet by the induced

$$\operatorname{div}(\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{div}}\widehat v) =(\det A)^{-1}(\widehat{\operatorname{div}}\widehat v)\circ F^{-1}.$$
The covariant Piola map
$\mathcal P_F^{\mathrm{curl}}\widehat v=A^{-T}\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$

$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Assume Countable Choice for the published Sobolev interfaces cited below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and use real scalars. $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ means the $d$-tuple of real $L^2$ equivalence classes, with norm $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|v_j\|_2^2$. The test space $C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ consists of real smooth functions compactly supported in $D$.

For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$, say that $g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)$ is its distributional divergence when
$$
\int_D v\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx=-\int_D g\phi\,dx\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R).
$$
The $L^2$ class $g$ is unique when it exists by uniqueness of weak derivatives ([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]). Define
$$
H(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d):\text{there is }g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)\text{ with }g=\operatorname{div}v\text{ distributionally}\},
$$
and equip it with the graph norm
$$
\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}:=\bigl(\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
$$
The Sobolev notation $H^1(D)=W^{1,2}(D)$ and $H^1_0(D)=W^{1,2}_0(D)$ uses the norm and zero-boundary closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. No pointwise boundary value is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. $$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$

abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.

This definition separates the property of the space from the particular map $\operatorname{id}_X$. The next corollary proves that it is equivalent to the familiar condition that the identity map be nullhomotopic.

For every $1\le k\le d$, the boundary maps of
[[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]] satisfy
$$\partial_{k-1}\circ\partial_k=0.$$

with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2.    is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

Let $X$ be a topological space. For each integer $n\geq 0$, a
**singular $n$-simplex in $X$** is a continuous map
$$\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$$
from the standard topological simplex of
[[def-standard-topological-simplex-and-its-affine-face-maps]]. Write
$S_n(X)$ for the set of all singular $n$-simplices in $X$.

The **singular chain group with integer coefficients** is the free abelian group
on $S_n(X)$:
$$C_n(X;\mathbb Z):=\bigoplus_{\sigma\in S_n(X)}\mathbb Z[\sigma].$$
Thus an element of $C_n(X;\mathbb Z)$ is a finite formal sum
$$\sum_{k=1}^m a_k\sigma_k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb Z,\ \sigma_k\in S_n(X).$$

If $G$ is an abelian group, the **singular chain group with coefficients in
$G$** is
$$C_n(X;G):=C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z} G,$$
using the tensor product of
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]. The page's
convention is that coefficients are attached through this tensor-product
construction, not by choosing a preferred $G$-basis of singular simplices.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.

used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.

finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

derivations.claim: If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$, [F12] gives $\Omega=\varnothing$; by [F1] and [F4] all real chain, cochain, and finite-element spaces are zero, and [F11] gives $H_k(\varnothing;\mathbb R)=0$. All cohomology and harmonic statements then reduce to the unique maps and decompositions of zero spaces, and the nonempty contractible branch is inapplicable. Suppose henceforth that $\mathcal T\ne\varnothing$. In degree zero, the vertex basis $\lambda_i$ is dual to vertex evaluation; a value at each vertex determines a unique affine function on each incident tetrahedron, and common-face traces agree because they agree at the face vertices. Thus $J^0:W_h^0\to C^0$ is a bijection. In degree one, [F2] makes the six local edge moments a bijection between each local Nedelec space and its six edge values. The definition of $N_h^1$ imposes one value for each globally oriented edge. Any global assignment therefore determines the unique local fields on each cell, and [F3] makes their assembly a global H(curl) field; conversely, zero global moments force every cell restriction to vanish by [F2]. Thus $J^1:N_h^1\to C^1$ is a bijection.

In degree two, the four oriented face fluxes determine each local $RT_0$ field by [F3]. The definition of $N_h^2$ imposes one value for every global oriented face; these values determine unique local fields and [F3] assembles them into a global H(div) field. Zero global fluxes force every local field to vanish, so $J^2:N_h^2\to C^2$ is a bijection. In degree three, a constant is determined by its cell integral, so $J^3:N_h^3\to C^3$ is a bijection.

The dual differential $\delta^k$ evaluates a cochain on the oriented boundary of each $(k+1)$-simplex. For $k=0$, its value on an oriented edge is the terminal nodal value minus the initial value; for $k=1$, its value on a face is the signed sum of its boundary-edge circulations; and for $k=2$, its value on a tetrahedron is the signed sum of its boundary-face fluxes. By [F3] these are exactly the degrees of freedom of $\nabla$, $\operatorname{curl}$, and $\operatorname{div}$. Thus $J^{k+1}d_h=\delta^kJ^k$ for each differential. By [F8], $\delta^{k+1}\delta^k=0$, so these maps are cochain complexes and the bijections induce isomorphisms on cohomology.

Write $Z_k=\ker\partial_k$ and $B_k=\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$; [F8] gives $B_k\subseteq Z_k$. Identify each cochain with its coordinate functional on the oriented simplex basis. Then $\ker\delta^k$ consists exactly of functionals vanishing on $B_k$, namely $B_k^\perp$. The image of $\delta^{k-1}=\partial_k^*$ lies in $Z_k^\perp$, since $(\partial_k^*\ell)(z)=\ell(\partial_kz)=0$ for $z\in Z_k$. These two subspaces have the same dimension: $\dim\operatorname{im}\partial_k^*=\operatorname{rank}\partial_k=\dim C_k-\dim Z_k=\dim Z_k^\perp$, so $\operatorname{im}\partial_k^*=Z_k^\perp$. Restricting a functional in $B_k^\perp$ to $Z_k$ therefore descends to $Z_k/B_k$ and has kernel $Z_k^\perp$. Every functional on $Z_k/B_k$ pulls back to a functional on $Z_k$ vanishing on $B_k$; extend a finite basis of $Z_k$ to one of $C_k$ and set the added basis values to zero. This proves surjectivity of restriction and hence $H^k(C^*)=B_k^\perp/Z_k^\perp\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(Z_k/B_k,\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(H_k^{\mathrm{simp}}(\mathcal T;\mathbb R),\mathbb R)$. Since these spaces are finite dimensional, their real duals have the same dimension.

By [F5], $H_k^{\mathrm{simp}}(\mathcal T;\mathbb R)\cong H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R)$. If $|\mathcal T|=\overline\Omega$ is nonempty, connected, and contractible in the sense of [F7], [F6] makes this group $\mathbb R$ for $k=0$ and zero for $k>0$. Steps 1.1–2.2 therefore show that the discrete cohomology is one-dimensional in degree zero and zero in positive degrees, which is exactness of the displayed finite sequence, including surjectivity of its last map. The globally constant functions lie in $W_h^0$ and have zero gradient, so the one-dimensional degree-zero kernel consists exactly of constants.

For arbitrary topology, let $Z_h^1=\ker\operatorname{curl}$ and $B_h^1=\nabla W_h^0$. By step 2.1, $B_h^1\subseteq Z_h^1$. The space $Z_h^1$ is finite dimensional as a subspace of $N_h^1$, so [F10] applied inside $Z_h^1$ gives $Z_h^1=B_h^1\oplus(Z_h^1\cap(B_h^1)^\perp)$ with orthogonality from [F9]. The second summand has dimension $\dim(Z_h^1/B_h^1)=\dim H^1(C^*)=\dim H_1(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R)$ by steps 2.1–2.2 and the duality proved in step 2.2. Applying the same [F10] argument to $Z_h^2=\ker\operatorname{div}$ and $B_h^2=\operatorname{curl}N_h^1\subseteq Z_h^2$ gives the asserted second harmonic space and dimension. These are discrete cohomology components, not an assertion that a continuum sequence is exact.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

Assume Countable Choice for the graph-space uniqueness and $L^2$ conventions of [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. Let $V_h=N_h^1$ be the lowest-order edge space on a finite tetrahedral mesh, as in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. It is finite dimensional: restriction to the finitely many cells injects it into the finite product of the local spaces, each spanned by at most six Whitney edge fields. Injectivity holds because the cells cover $\Omega$ up to their measure-zero facets. Use the componentwise real $L^2$ inner product defined in [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. Define its curl kernel and the $L^2$ gauge space by
$$K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{curl}v_h=0\},\qquad Z_h:=V_h\cap K_h^\perp.$$
The quotient $\dot V_h:=V_h/K_h$ has norm $\|[v_h]\|_{\operatorname{curl}}:=\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$; this is well-defined and positive definite because two representatives differ by an element of $K_h$. The bilinear form induced by curl-curl is $a_h([u_h],[v_h])=(\operatorname{curl}u_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2}$. A representative of a quotient solution is fixed by the gauge condition $u_h\in Z_h$. The mixed gauge system uses a multiplier $p_h\in K_h$:
$$a_h(u_h,v_h)+(p_h,v_h)_{L^2}=f(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad (u_h,q_h)_{L^2}=0\quad(q_h\in K_h).$$
The quotient energy norm, rather than the full $H(\operatorname{curl})$ norm, is the norm controlled by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice for the graph spaces and real $L^2$ product as in [[def-na-curl-curl-kernel-quotient-gauge]]. Let $V_h$ be that finite-dimensional real edge space, $K_h=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{V_h})$, and $Z_h=V_h\cap K_h^\perp$. Here $V_h^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(V_h,\mathbb R)$ is the algebraic dual of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. For every $f\in V_h^*$ there is a unique pair $(u_h,p_h)\in Z_h\times K_h$ satisfying
$$ (\operatorname{curl}u_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2}+(p_h,v_h)_{L^2}=f(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad (u_h,q_h)_{L^2}=0\quad(q_h\in K_h).$$
The gauge multiplier is the $L^2$ Riesz representative of $f|_{K_h}$. The quotient solution satisfies the exact stability identity
$$\|\operatorname{curl}u_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{Z_h}\|_{(Z_h,\|\operatorname{curl}(\cdot)\|_{L^2})^*},\qquad \|p_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{K_h}\|_{(K_h,\|\cdot\|_{L^2})^*}.$$
The constraint form $b(v,q)=(v,q)_{L^2}$ has inf-sup constant one when $K_h\ne\{0\}$, $V_h$ has the $H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph norm and $K_h$ has the $L^2$ norm; if $K_h=\{0\}$ the constraint is vacuous. The curl form is coercive with constant one on $Z_h$ in the quotient curl norm. No mesh-uniform estimate in the full graph norm is claimed here.

statement.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Assume Countable Choice for the H(curl), H(div), and real $L^2$ inner-product interfaces used here; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed. Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching tetrahedral mesh with realization $|\mathcal T|=\overline\Omega$. Define $C_k(\mathcal T;\mathbb R)$ by extending the oriented chain groups of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]] to real coefficients, and put $C^k=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k,\mathbb R)$ with coboundary $\delta^k=\partial_{k+1}^*$. The degrees of freedom give a cochain isomorphism from
$$W_h^0\xrightarrow{\nabla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$$
to $C^0\xrightarrow{\delta^0}C^1\xrightarrow{\delta^1}C^2\xrightarrow{\delta^2}C^3$. Consequently the discrete cohomology in degree $k$ is naturally isomorphic to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R),\mathbb R)$. If $\overline\Omega$ is nonempty, connected, and contractible, then the sequence is exact at every positive-degree space, $\ker\nabla$ consists of constants, and $\operatorname{div}:N_h^2\to N_h^3$ is onto. For general topology, define
$$\mathcal H_h^1:=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{N_h^1})\cap(\nabla W_h^0)^\perp,\qquad \mathcal H_h^2:=\ker(\operatorname{div}|_{N_h^2})\cap(\operatorname{curl}N_h^1)^\perp$$
using the $L^2$ inner product. Then $\ker\operatorname{curl}=\nabla W_h^0\oplus\mathcal H_h^1$ and $\ker\operatorname{div}=\operatorname{curl}N_h^1\oplus\mathcal H_h^2$, with $\dim\mathcal H_h^k=\dim H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R)$ for $k=1,2$.

   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$
If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then $f^*=g^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

For a topological space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, the singular chain groups
and boundary maps of [[def-singular-boundary-operator]] form the
**singular chain complex**
$$C_\bullet(X;G):=\bigl(\cdots\to C_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\partial_n}C_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots\bigr),$$
because [[thm-the-singular-boundary-squares-to-zero]] gives
$\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$.

Its degree-$n$ cycles and boundaries are
$$Z_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G):=\ker\partial_n,\qquad B_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G):=\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1},$$
in the sense of [[def-cycle-and-boundary-subobjects-of-a-complex]].

The **$n$th singular homology group** is the homology object of this chain
complex:
$$H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G):=Z_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\big/B_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G),$$
equivalently $H_n(C_\bullet(X;G))$ in the notation of
[[def-homology-object-of-a-chain-complex]]. When the coefficient group is
$\mathbb Z$, write simply $C_n(X)$ and $H_n(X)$ when no confusion can arise.

For a space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, a degree-$n$ **singular cocycle** is a cochain in $Z^n(X;G)=\ker\delta^n$ and a degree-$n$ **singular coboundary** belongs to $B^n(X;G)=\operatorname{im}\delta^{n-1}$, for the positive coboundary convention of [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]]. The square-zero lemma [[lem-the-singular-coboundary-squares-to-zero]] implies $B^n\subseteq Z^n$: if $\varphi=\delta^{n-1}\psi$, then $\delta^n\varphi=0$.

The **singular cohomology group with coefficients in $G$** is
$$H^n(X;G)=Z^n(X;G)/B^n(X;G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad H^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0).$$
This is the abelian quotient with addition $[\varphi]+[\psi]=[\varphi+\psi]$: changing either representative by a coboundary changes the sum by a coboundary. Thus two cocycles represent the same class exactly when their difference is $\delta^{n-1}\eta$ for some degree-$(n-1)$ cochain $\eta$. In degree zero, $B^0=0$ because $C^{-1}=0$; hence $H^0=\ker\delta^0$. The zero convention in negative degrees agrees with the same kernel/image construction on the zero cochain groups.

If coefficients are a module over a commutative ring, the same groups and maps are modules and linear maps, and this is their module quotient. Empty $X$ or zero coefficients give zero cohomology in every degree. The notation does not define cohomology as the dual of homology; such identifications require their own theorems. No choice of cocycle representatives and no AC is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Put $M=\overline\Omega$. It is compact by boundedness and closedness. Near each boundary point a Lipschitz graph chart $x_3=\phi(x')$ straightens $M$ by the explicit homeomorphism $(x',x_3)\mapsto(x',x_3-\phi(x'))$ to a closed halfspace neighborhood. Interior points use Euclidean balls. These charts show that $M$ is a Hausdorff second-countable three-manifold with topological boundary exactly $\partial\Omega$ and interior exactly $\Omega$. Its orientation is the standard Euclidean orientation on its interior; this is precisely the orientation convention for manifolds with boundary in [F2]. By [F1], $\Omega\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. Contractibility of $\Omega$, [F3], and factorization through a point give $H^2(M;\mathbb R)=0$: the point has one singular simplex in each degree, and its real cochain differentials are successively zero and identity, so its positive cohomology is zero. Also $M$ is path connected: its interior is path connected by contractibility, and a half-chart path joins any boundary point to its interior. The augmentation identifies $H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R$, because any difference of points is the boundary of a path and every zero-chain of coefficient sum zero is a finite linear combination of such differences. The boundary is nonempty: a ray from any interior point eventually leaves the bounded set and its first exit point is a boundary point.

By [F2], $H_1(M,\partial M;\mathbb R)=0$. The exact sequence in [F3] then makes $H_0(\partial M;\mathbb R)\to H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ injective. The boundary is a two-manifold by the graph charts, hence locally path connected, so its connected components are path components. If there were two, choose one point in each. Their difference is nonzero in $H_0(\partial M;\mathbb R)$: the sum of coefficients on the first path component defines a linear functional on zero-chains which kills every one-simplex boundary, yet sends this difference to one. Its image in $H_0(M;\mathbb R)$ is zero since the two points are joined by a path in $M$, contradicting injectivity. Therefore the nonempty boundary is connected. No finite-element incidence matrix is used to infer this continuum topological claim.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded, convex and nonempty, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n)\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Here $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx$ is the mean of $u$ over $\Omega$,
which is well defined because $\Omega$ is nonempty open and bounded. The proof
below gives the explicit choice
$$C(n)=\frac{2\,(2^n-1)}{n},$$
which depends only on the dimension; no dependence on $p$, on the shape of
$\Omega$, on $|\Omega|$ or on the regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y

u.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure
$\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$.

derivations.claim: It suffices first to treat the special graph $G=\{(x',x_3):x_3>\phi(x')\}$, with $\phi$ globally $L$-Lipschitz. A local graph extends to a global graph without increasing $L$ by $\phi(x')=\inf_{y'}(\phi(y')+L|x'-y'|)$, taking $y'$ over the original graph base; for $L=0$ use the same constant. Localized input will have support strictly inside the original chart. The construction for $G$ is truncated at side length one, which fixes an inhomogeneous length scale. Rotations, translations, and a fixed dilation transfer it to any chart scale.

Decompose $G^c\setminus\partial G$ into maximal dyadic cubes $Q$ for which $20\sqrt3\ell_Q\le\operatorname{dist}(Q,\partial G)$. Cubes of sufficiently small size containing any given exterior point satisfy this condition, while large ancestors fail, so maximal cubes exist and cover the exterior, with disjoint interiors. Failure for the parent and the triangle inequality give $20\sqrt3\ell_Q\le\operatorname{dist}(Q,\partial G)\le C\ell_Q$. For two cubes whose $9/8$ enlargements meet, the distance function is 1-Lipschitz; these two inequalities imply $C_0^{-1}\ell_Q\le\ell_R\le C_0\ell_Q$, with a dimension-only $C_0$, and boundedly many such neighbors by volume packing. The enlarged cubes have bounded overlap for the same reason. Pick a fixed nonnegative smooth bump supported in the $9/8$ enlargement of the unit cube and positive on the closed unit cube; rescale it to $\eta_Q$ and put $\theta_Q=\eta_Q/(\sum_R\eta_R)$. The denominator is bounded below, only boundedly many comparable scales meet, and differentiation of this quotient gives $|D^j\theta_Q|\le C_j\ell_Q^{-j}$ for $j=0,1,2$. Thus $(\theta_Q)$ is a locally finite smooth partition on the exterior.

Restrictions of smooth functions defined in a neighborhood of $\overline G$ are dense in $H^m(G)$ for $m=1,2$. First cut off at large radius, with convergence in $H^m$ by the product rule and integrable tails. For the resulting compactly supported $f$, translate inward: $f_t(x)=f(x+t e_3)$ is defined on the neighborhood $G-t e_3$ of $\overline G$. Each derivative on $G$ is the restriction of the corresponding derivative of $f$, extended by zero merely as an $L^2$ function and translated; [F2] therefore gives convergence to $D^\alpha f$ in $L^2(G)$ as $t\downarrow0$. Convolve $f_t$ with a mollifier of radius $\varepsilon<t/(2(1+L))$. Every ball used at a point of $\overline G$ stays inside $G-t e_3$, so differentiation under the convolution is legitimate there. [F2] gives convergence of all these derivatives, by choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small after $t$. Fixed cutoffs retain compact support. This proves the asserted density without assuming an extension theorem.

Write $\delta_Q=\phi(a_Q')-a_{Q,3}$. Distance to a Lipschitz graph and vertical distance satisfy $\operatorname{dist}(a_Q,\partial G)\le\delta_Q\le\sqrt{1+L^2}\operatorname{dist}(a_Q,\partial G)$: the second inequality follows by comparing to any graph point and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to $L|a_Q'-b'|+|a_{Q,3}-\phi(b')|$. Hence $c\ell_Q\le\delta_Q\le C_L\ell_Q$. Fix $A>2C_L+100(1+L)$ and let $Q^*$ be the cube of side $\ell_Q$ centered at $b_Q=a_Q+A\ell_Q e_3$. It lies in $G$, its distance to the graph is between $c_L\ell_Q$ and $C_L'\ell_Q$, and $\operatorname{dist}(Q,Q^*)\le A\ell_Q$. The cubes $Q^*$ have bounded overlap: at any point in one of them their scale is comparable to its distance from the graph, and their original disjoint cubes lie in a ball of radius $C_L\ell_Q$.

For neighboring exterior cubes $Q,R$, their interior cubes $Q^*,R^*$ can be joined by a chain of a bounded number (depending only on $L$) of interior cubes of sides comparable to $\ell_Q$, with consecutive overlaps containing a cube of side $c_L\ell_Q$. Here is an explicit construction. Join $b_Q$ vertically upward to height $H=\max(b_{Q,3},b_{R,3})+L|b_Q'-b_R'|+10\sqrt3\max(\ell_Q,\ell_R)$, then horizontally to the vertical line through $b_R$, then vertically down to $b_R$. Each segment stays above the graph by at least $c_L\ell_Q$, has length at most $C_L\ell_Q$, and stays at distance at most $C_L\ell_Q$ from the graph. Subdivide these segments into steps of length $b\ell_Q/4$, and use centered cubes of side $b\ell_Q$, with $b>0$ small enough to lie in $G$; append $Q^*,R^*$ as endpoints. Call the union $B_{QR}$. These bridges have bounded overlap when all neighbor pairs are considered: every point in a bridge has graph distance comparable to its scale, and all corresponding exterior cubes are disjoint cubes of comparable size in a fixed multiple of a ball of that scale. There are boundedly many of them by volume packing.

For $\ell_Q\le1$ put $P_Q f(x)=f_{Q^*}+(
abla f)_{Q^*}\cdot(x-b_Q)$, an affine polynomial determined linearly by the $H^1$ class. Put $P_Q=0$ when $\ell_Q>1$. For an interior cube $S$ of side $s$ and center $c_S$, write $P_Sf=f_S+(
abla f)_S\cdot(x-c_S)$. Applying [F1] first to $
abla f$ and then to $f-P_Sf$, whose mean is zero, gives $\|f-P_Sf\|_{L^2(S)}\le Cs^2\|D^2f\|_{L^2(S)}$ and $\|
abla(f-P_Sf)\|_{L^2(S)}\le Cs\|D^2f\|_{L^2(S)}$ for $H^2$ data. For merely $H^1$ data, $\|f-P_Sf\|_{L^2(S)}\le Cs\|
abla f\|_{L^2(S)}$. These estimates also hold on the finite cube chains in step 4.1, with constants depending on their uniform chain geometry. To see the latter assertion without assuming a chain Poincare theorem, compare the polynomials on each consecutive overlap. For consecutive chain cubes $S,T$, choose a cube $O\subset S\cap T$ of side $ho\asymp s$. On $O$ the triangle inequality gives $\|P_Sf-P_Tf\|_{L^2(O)}\le\|f-P_Sf\|_{L^2(S)}+\|f-P_Tf\|_{L^2(T)}$, so the already proved residual bounds apply on the actual cubes $S,T$, without assuming their union lies in another interior cube. If an affine polynomial is $P(x)=a+b\cdot(x-c_O)$ on $O$, direct integration gives $\|P\|_{L^2(O)}^2=ho^3|a|^2+ho^5|b|^2/12$. Since the exterior target cube $Q$ has side comparable to $s$ and lies within distance $C_Ls$ of each chain cube, this formula gives $\|D^jP\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C_Ls^{-j}\|P\|_{L^2(O)}$ for $j=0,1$, while $D^2P=0$. Apply it to $P_Sf-P_Tf$ and telescope along the chain. There are boundedly many links, so summing those finitely many bounds proves, for $Q,R$ neighbors with both scales at most one, $\|D^j(P_Qf-P_Rf)\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C\ell_Q^{m-j}\|D^mf\|_{L^2(B_{QR})},\qquad 0\le j\le m,\quad m=1,2.$ Here $D^2$ of an affine polynomial is zero; $B_{QR}$ may be enlarged by the finitely many overlapping chain cubes used in the comparison, retaining step 4.1's overlap property.

Define $Ef=f$ on $G$ and $Ef=\sum_Q	heta_Q P_Qf$ on its exterior. For an exterior cube $Q$, subtract $P_Q$ inside the sum and differentiate. For second derivatives, all terms containing $D^2P_Q$ vanish, and derivatives of the partition of total order one or two multiply derivatives of $P_R-P_Q$. Step 5.1 bounds their $L^2(Q)$ norm by $C\sum_{R\sim Q}\|D^2f\|_{L^2(B_{QR})}$. For first derivatives, the remaining term $
abla P_Q$ is bounded by the average of $
abla f$ on $Q^*$, and the residual terms are bounded by the $m=1$ version of step 5.1. For the zeroth derivative, $\|P_Q\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C(\|f\|_{L^2(Q^*)}+\ell_Q\|
abla f\|_{L^2(Q^*)})$. Cubes with $\ell_Q>1$ have zero polynomial; if a neighbor is nonzero, all scales involved lie between $C_0^{-1}$ and $C_0$, so one bounds its polynomial and both its derivatives directly by $C\|f\|_{H^m(R^*)}$ instead of a difference estimate. Summing squares, using bounded neighbor counts and the bounded overlap of interior cubes and bridges, proves $\|Ef\|_{H^m(G)}+\|Ef\|_{H^m(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline G)}\le C\|f\|_{H^m(G)},\qquad m=1,2,$ where the norms on the right are taken only when defined. This estimates derivatives separately on the two open sides; the next steps verify that there is no boundary distribution.

For such smooth $f$, use a fixed ambient smooth continuation near the graph to compare with $Ef$. At an exterior point $x$ at distance $d$ from the graph, every active cube has $\ell_Q\asymp d$ and $Q^*$ is within distance $C_Ld$ of $x$. Taylor's formula and the affine reproduction of $P_Q$ therefore give $|Ef(x)-f(x)|\le C_f d^2$ and $|\nabla(Ef-f)(x)|\le C_f d$ on compact neighborhoods of the graph. To verify the weak derivatives across the graph, define on the exterior $\rho(x)=\sum_Q\theta_Q(x)\ell_Q$. Local finiteness makes $\rho$ smooth there. At each exterior point the active cube sizes are comparable to $d$, so $c d\le\rho\le Cd$. Since $\sum_Q\theta_Q=1$, differentiating after subtracting one active scale gives $|\nabla\rho|\le C$ and $|D^2\rho|\le C/d$, using $|D^j\theta_Q|\le C_j\ell_Q^{-j}$ and the bounded number of active cubes. Choose a smooth scalar cutoff $\zeta$ that is zero on $(-\infty,1]$ and one on $[2,\infty)$, and put $\chi_t(x)=\zeta(\rho(x)/t)$ outside, extended by zero across $\partial G$. This is smooth across the boundary because it vanishes in a full exterior collar. On its transition strip, $d\asymp t$ and the chain rule gives $|D\chi_t|\le C/t$ and $|D^2\chi_t|\le C/t^2$. In a graph chart, the vertical gap $\delta=|x_3-\phi(x')|$ satisfies $\delta\le\sqrt{1+L^2}\,d$: compare $x$ to any graph point and use the Lipschitz bound on $\phi$, then take the infimum. Thus on a compact chart the strip $d<Ct$ has vertical sections of length at most $C't$, so its volume is $O(t)$ by [F5]. The product-rule errors from $h=Ef-f$ on that strip satisfy $|h|=O(t^2)$ and $|Dh|=O(t)$, so $hD\chi_t$, $DhD\chi_t$, and $hD^2\chi_t$ tend to zero in $L^2$; the omitted piecewise second derivatives tend to zero in $L^2$ by absolute continuity of their squared integrals. Thus the cutoffs converge in $H^2$ locally and prove that the zero-inside function has precisely the piecewise weak derivatives, with no boundary distribution. The same argument with only first derivatives proves the $H^1$ assertion. Consequently step 6.1 is a genuine whole-space Sobolev bound for the smooth dense class.

For arbitrary $H^m$ data take the smooth approximating sequence in step 2.2. The bound in step 6.1 and step 7.1 makes its extensions Cauchy in the complete whole-space $H^m$ norm. Their limit equals the original input on $G$. On each exterior cube its formula equals the displayed averaged-polynomial formula, since the finitely many local averages and derivatives entering that formula converge. Thus the $H^1$ and $H^2$ extensions are the same operator on their common domain, rather than two incompatible choices. This completes the special graph case.

For bounded $D$, cover its compact boundary by finitely many graph charts and choose smooth cutoffs supported strictly inside them, together with an interior cutoff, summing to one near $\overline D$. Each localized function is extended by zero within its special graph outside its original chart; since its cutoff vanishes near the chart sides, this is an $H^m$ function on the graph with the expected product derivatives. Apply the graph operator, then multiply the result by a second fixed cutoff supported in the chart and equal to one on the first cutoff's support. On $D$ the result is the localized original function, including the part where that function is zero. The interior term is extended by zero, with no interface near its support. Summing these finitely many extensions gives $E$, preserves the restriction identity, and gives both asserted boundedness estimates by the weak product rule. A final cutoff equal to one near $\overline D$ confines support. Finite graph covers work equally for disconnected $D$; no connectivity or topology is used. All construction coefficients are fixed independently of $f$. This proves the statement.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
