derivations.claim: Shape regularity bounds every cell's solid angle at each vertex below and bounds the ratio of its edge lengths above. Consequently at most a fixed number of cells meet a vertex. Their link is connected through faces containing that vertex: in an interior star the link is a triangulated sphere, and in a boundary star it is a triangulated disk, since a Lipschitz graph has a ball or half-ball neighborhood. Across a shared face the two diameters are comparable because the face edges are comparable to each diameter. A face path in the link has bounded length, so every two cells meeting a vertex have comparable diameters, with a constant depending only on shape regularity. Assign $g_h(v)=\min_{K\ni v}h_K$ at every vertex and interpolate affinely. Barycentric differentiation and $|\nabla\lambda_v|\le C/h_K$ give the asserted cellwise comparability and gradient bound.

In a boundary graph box choose its upward unit direction $e_j$. Shrink its support neighborhood so that every planar boundary piece meeting that neighborhood has outward normal $n$ satisfying $n\cdot e_j\le-\alpha_j<0$. This holds because for a graph $x_3=f(x')$, with the domain above it, every outward unit normal is $(\nabla f,-1)/(1+|\nabla f|^2)^{1/2}$. Refine the finite boundary cover by finitely many concentric ball pairs whose larger closures lie in the assigned graph boxes and whose smaller balls still cover the compact boundary. Use [F1] to put a bump $\beta_j$ in each larger ball, equal to one on its smaller ball. On the open collar where $S=\sum_j\beta_j>0$, put $\chi_j=\beta_j/S$ and $b_0=\sum_j\chi_j e_j$. A compact-set cutoff $\eta$ supported in that collar and equal to one on a smaller collar gives the global smooth field $b=\eta b_0$, extended by zero away from the support of $\eta$. This is an explicitly normalized finite partition; no arbitrary-index partition theorem or choice axiom is imported. At each collar point every participating $e_j$ has the strict inward inequality for every nearby boundary face, so their convex combination does too, uniformly. After shrinking the collar, there is $r>0$ such that $b(x)+r y$ is strictly inward for all nearby faces and $-b(x)+r y$ strictly outward, for every $|y|\le1$.

A bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedron is quasiconvex: close points in one boundary graph box can be joined by two vertical segments and a horizontal segment above the graph, of total length at most a fixed multiple of their distance; interior balls have the same property. A finite smaller cover gives this assertion for sufficiently close points. For remaining pairs, join the finitely many box centers through fixed interior polygonal paths and divide their bounded length by the fixed positive distance threshold. Componentwise the same argument applies to a disconnected domain, and distinct components have positive separation. Integrating the cellwise gradient along these paths gives the mesh-independent Euclidean Lipschitz bound for $g_h$. Extend it to a neighborhood by the explicit formula $\widetilde g_h(x)=\inf_{z\in\overline\Omega}(g_h(z)+L|x-z|)$, then truncate above by $\max g_h$; this is positive and $L$-Lipschitz and agrees on $\overline\Omega$.

Here are the distance assertions, including concave corners. In any one graph box write $a=b(x)+r y$. Along the horizontal segment from $x'$ to $x'+\tau a'$, the graph is piecewise affine; on each piece the preceding normal inequality gives $a_3-\nabla f\cdot a'\ge\beta>0$. Integration along that segment gives $f(x'+\tau a')\le f(x')+\tau a_3-\beta\tau$. Thus for $x\in\overline\Omega$ the point $x+\tau a$ lies above the graph by at least $\beta\tau$, and its distance to the graph is at least $\beta\tau/(1+L^2)^{1/2}$. Replacing $b$ by $-b$ reverses the inequality and puts boundary points strictly below the graph. The finite cover supplies uniform constants and a uniform allowed $\tau$. Away from the collar, small displacements remain inside. Substitute $\tau=tg_h(x)$; the upper bound on $g_h$ is at most the domain diameter. Thus one fixed $\epsilon_0$ works for every mesh.

Let $\omega_K$ be the union of cells sharing a vertex with $K$. The sum $\psi_K$ of the four global nodal hat functions for the vertices of $K$ is one on $K$, zero outside $\omega_K$, and has cellwise gradient at most $C/h_K$: every cell where it is nonzero shares a vertex with $K$, so step 1.1 applies. The path argument of step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Lip}(\psi_K)\le C_\Omega/h_K$. Hence $\operatorname{dist}(K,\Omega\setminus\omega_K)\ge c_\Omega h_K$. The number of cells in each patch and the number of patches containing one cell are bounded by the vertex-incidence bound. This proves the claimed neighborhood and overlap properties for sufficiently small displacements, including on graded meshes.

The displacement field $g_h(\pm b+r y)$ has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, since $g_h$, $b$ and their Lipschitz constants are uniformly bounded. Reduce $\epsilon_0$ so this constant times $\epsilon_0$ is below $1/2$. Then $\frac12|x-z|\le|F_{t,y}^{\pm}(x)-F_{t,y}^{\pm}(z)|\le\frac32|x-z|$. The displacement is at most $Ct h_K$ on $K$. Step 3.1 now proves the patch assertion, and step 2.2 proves the interior and exterior boundary assertions.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

derivations.claim: Since $U$ is supported in $A$, Holder gives $\|U\|_1\le |A|^{1/2}\|U\|_2$, and therefore $|\widehat U(\xi)|\le |A|^{1/2}\|U\|_2$. For $\xi\ne0$ define $\widehat p(\xi)=\frac{\xi\cdot\widehat U(\xi)}{2\pi i|\xi|^2},\qquad \widehat w(\xi)=\widehat U(\xi)-\frac{\xi(\xi\cdot\widehat U(\xi))}{|\xi|^2}.$ Set both values at zero arbitrarily, for instance zero. The multiplier defining $\widehat w$ is an orthogonal projection in $\mathbb C^3$, so $\|\widehat w\|_2\le\|\widehat U\|_2$, and $2\pi i\xi\widehat p$ is the complementary orthogonal projection of $\widehat U$. At $|\xi|<1$, $|\widehat p|^2\le (4\pi^2)^{-1}|A|\|U\|_2^2|\xi|^{-2}$, whose integral is finite in dimension three; at $|\xi|\ge1$ it is bounded by $(4\pi^2)^{-1}|\widehat U|^2$. Thus $p\in H^1$ and $\|p\|_{H^1}\le C_A\|U\|_2$ by [F1]. This is the essential low-frequency check; an arbitrary nonsupported $L^2$ field would not give it.

The vector identity $|\xi|^2|\widehat w|^2=|\xi\times\widehat U|^2$ and the multiplier identity for curl give $\int4\pi^2|\xi|^2|\widehat w|^2=\|\operatorname{curl}U\|_2^2$. Hence $w\in H^1$, with the asserted derivative norm. The displayed Fourier definitions give $U=w+\nabla p$, $\xi\cdot\widehat w=0$, and $\xi\times\widehat w=\xi\times\widehat U$, so all asserted distributional identities follow by Fourier injectivity. Finally $\widehat U(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat U(\xi)}$ for real $U$. The two definitions have the corresponding conjugate symmetry (including the sign of $i$ in $\widehat p$); uniqueness of the inverse transform therefore gives real $p,w$. Every operation is linear, and [F1] supplies all norm claims.

$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let

$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

derivations.claim: Let $B=B(a,r)\Subset G$ and choose $r'>r$ with $B(a,r')\Subset G$. Zero-extend $v|_{B(a,r')}$ as an $L^2$ function and convolve at radii $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$ smaller than $r'-r$. The resulting $v_j$ are smooth and curl free on a neighborhood of $B$, and $v_j\to v$ in $L^2(B)$ by [F2]. Put $g_j(x)=\int_0^1 v_j(a+t(x-a))\cdot(x-a)\,dt$. The smooth curl-free identity $\partial_iv_{j,k}=\partial_kv_{j,i}$ gives $\partial_i g_j=\int_0^1\frac{d}{dt}(t v_{j,i}(a+t(x-a)))dt=v_{j,i}(x)$. Subtract $(g_j)_B$. For any $j,k$, [F1] bounds the $H^1$ norm of this normalized difference by $C_B\|v_j-v_k\|_{L^2(B)}$. Completeness gives a limit $g_B\in H^1(B)$ with mean zero and gradient $v$. No passage through smooth de Rham cohomology is made.

Cover $G$ by its countable rational balls with compact closure in $G$, and choose the primitives in step 1.1. Every nonempty intersection of two such balls is convex and connected. By [F3], $g_B-g_C=c_{BC}$ almost everywhere on $B\cap C$, with a unique real constant; $c_{BC}=-c_{CB}$, and $c_{BC}+c_{CD}=c_{BD}$ whenever the triple intersection is nonempty. Consider a germ of a primitive to mean a local $H^1$ primitive on a neighborhood of a point, identifying two when they agree almost everywhere on a smaller neighborhood. Fix one germ at a basepoint. Along a path, choose a finite subdivision whose successive subpaths lie in balls, and transport the current primitive by adding the unique constant needed to agree on an overlap at each subdivision point. This defines the terminal germ. Inserting extra subdivision points does not change it, and changing the covering balls gives the same result: refine around every subdivision point so that all balls compared contain that point, use their nonempty open intersections, and use the displayed cocycle identity. Thus transport is well defined along a path and reverses under reversal of that path.

Transport is invariant under endpoint-fixed path homotopy. For a continuous homotopy $H:[0,1]^2\to G$, compactness gives a finite subcover of its image by the ball cover and a Lebesgue number for the pullback cover of the square. A sufficiently fine rectangular grid then maps every closed cell into one ball. The transport around the boundary of that cell is the identity: compute it with that one ball's primitive; subdivision and ball independence from step 2.1 permit this computation. Compose these identities over all cells. Every interior edge is traversed once in each direction, so its transports cancel. The two vertical boundary paths are constant when endpoints are fixed; hence the transports along the two horizontal paths agree. If $G$ has the stated loop property, any two paths from the basepoint to a given point have equal terminal germs by applying this argument to their concatenation with one reversed. A connected open subset of Euclidean space is path connected: the set reachable by polygonal paths is both open and relatively closed, since a ball about any point joins that point to all nearby points. Thus there is a terminal germ at every point.

On a small ball around any point, path independence identifies these terminal germs with one fixed local primitive plus a constant. The resulting local functions therefore agree almost everywhere on overlaps. They define an $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ class on $G$: enumerate the countable ball cover and use the first applicable representative on each measurable difference of balls; the overlap exceptional sets have countable union of measure zero. Any compact subset has a finite ball subcover, so the class is $H^1$ locally, and its weak derivative is $v$ there and hence globally on compactly supported tests. This is $f$. Any two choices differ by a locally $H^1$ zero-gradient function, so [F3] makes the difference constant. AC is used only for the cited analytic interfaces and the countable local representative/primitive choices.

Let $X$ be a contractible topological space and let $x_0\in X$. Then
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is the trivial group.

Assume AC. Let $G\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open connected set, and let $v\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(G;\mathbb R^3)$ have zero distributional curl. Every ball compactly contained in $G$ has an $H^1$ primitive of $v$. If every based loop in $G$ is homotopic to a constant loop fixing its basepoint, these local primitives glue to $f\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(G)$ with $\nabla f=v$. Such $f$ is unique up to a constant. This assertion alone does not assert global $L^2$ integrability of $f$ on $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

   $\hat v_i$ be measurable representatives of $u$ and $D_iu$. Define

derivations.claim: By [F1] choose $f\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ with $\nabla f=u$. It remains to prove global integrability; local weak exactness alone is insufficient. Fix a ball $B\Subset\Omega$. For $M>0$ let $f_M=\max(-M,\min(f,M))$. By [F3] locally, $f_M\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, $|\nabla f_M|\le|u|$, and $|f_M|\le M$. Since $\Omega$ has finite measure, these local derivative identities give global $H^1(\Omega)$ membership: the function is globally $L^2$, its locally specified derivatives are globally $L^2$, and every compactly supported test uses only finitely many local identities. Thus [F2] gives $\|f_M-(f_M)_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_2$.

Put $a_M=(f_M)_\Omega$ and $b_M=(f_M)_B$. The preceding estimate gives $|a_M-b_M|\le |B|^{-1/2}C_\Omega\|u\|_2$. Therefore $\|f_M-b_M\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega(1+|\Omega|^{1/2}|B|^{-1/2})\|u\|_2.$ On $B$, $f\in L^2$ and $|f_M|\le|f|$, so dominated convergence gives $b_M\to f_B$. Along the integers $M\to\infty$, $f_M\to f$ almost everywhere; Fatou's lemma applied to the displayed bound yields $f-f_B\in L^2(\Omega)$. Its weak gradient is $u\in L^2$, hence $p=f-f_B\in H^1(\Omega)$. If two such $p$ exist, their difference has zero weak gradient, and [F3] makes it constant on connected $\Omega$. This proves every original analytic and geometric clause.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used through the cited Countable-Choice and
Dependent-Choice interfaces (completed-product Fubini, approximate identities,
the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions), for
the countable selections of cutoffs and mollifier scales below, and through the
earlier ACL reconstruction lemma. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
open, $n\ge1$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
For an almost-everywhere class $u$ on $\Omega$ the following are equivalent:

1. $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$;
2. $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $u$ has one measurable ACL representative
   $u^*$ whose classical coordinate derivatives $\partial_i u^*$ exist almost
   everywhere, are measurable, and belong to $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

In that case $\partial_i u^*$ is a representative of $D_i u$ for every
$i$, that is, $D_i u=\partial_i u^*$ almost everywhere.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, there is only the zero class, its representative
$u^*=0$ is ACL, and every displayed assertion holds vacuously.

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with

almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,

$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

multiplier for this global conclusion.

pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let

1. An $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ class $F$ that vanishes almost everywhere outside $\overline\Omega$ restricts to $H_0^1(\Omega)$, and every $H_0^1(\Omega)$ class has an $H^1$ zero extension.
2. If $f\in H^1(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and $f=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $f\in H_0^1(\Omega)$.
3. The zero extension $U$ of $u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ belongs to $H(\operatorname{curl};\mathbb R^3)$, with $\operatorname{curl}U$ equal to the zero extension of $\operatorname{curl}u$; both component norms are preserved. Also $\nabla H_0^1(\Omega)\subset H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and its elements have zero curl.

Assume AC. Let $U\in H(\operatorname{curl};\mathbb R^3)$ be real and supported in a fixed bounded measurable set $A$ of finite measure. There are real fields $w\in H^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $p\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ depending linearly on $U$ such that $U=w+\nabla p$, $\operatorname{div}w=0$, $\operatorname{curl}w=\operatorname{curl}U$, and
$$\|w\|_2\le\|U\|_2,\qquad \|\nabla w\|_2=\|\operatorname{curl}U\|_2,\qquad \|p\|_{H^1}\le C_A\|U\|_2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

No contractibility, connected boundary, or mesh hypothesis is required. The scalar estimate uses the full H(curl) norm; no estimate by curl alone is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary.

1. An $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ class $F$ that vanishes almost everywhere outside $\overline\Omega$ restricts to $H_0^1(\Omega)$, and every $H_0^1(\Omega)$ class has an $H^1$ zero extension.
2. If $f\in H^1(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and $f=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $f\in H_0^1(\Omega)$.
3. The zero extension $U$ of $u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ belongs to $H(\operatorname{curl};\mathbb R^3)$, with $\operatorname{curl}U$ equal to the zero extension of $\operatorname{curl}u$; both component norms are preserved. Also $\nabla H_0^1(\Omega)\subset H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and its elements have zero curl.

All statements apply componentwise to vector fields where appropriate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded connected contractible Lipschitz polyhedron. If $u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has distributional curl zero, then there is $p\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $u=\nabla p$ almost everywhere; $p$ is unique up to an additive constant.

Assume AC. A nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ has nonempty connected boundary. In particular the connected-boundary clause of the regular-decomposition theorem follows from the domain assumptions in the discrete-compactness theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Ω\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. If
$u\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$$D_i u=0\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega\qquad(1\le i\le n),$$
then for every connected component $C$ of $\Omega$ there is a constant
$c_C\in\mathbb K$ such that $u=c_C$ almost everywhere on $C$. The empty
domain has no components, so its conclusion is vacuous.

The proof assumes full AC as stated, but uses it only through Countable Choice
for the Sobolev representative, Lebesgue, and mollification interfaces cited
below. No full-AC selection is made in the ball propagation argument.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$, $B=B(x_0,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $r>0$, $1\le p<\infty$, and $u\in W^{1,p}(B;\mathbb K)$ with ball average $u_B=|B|^{-1}\int_Bu$. Then $\|u-u_B\|_{L^p(B)}\le C(n,p)\,r\,\|Du\|_{L^p(B)}$.

Assume countable choice. On complex $L^2$, $\mathcal F_2^2f=Rf$, $Rf(x)=f(-x)$, and $\mathcal F_2^{-1}=R\mathcal F_2$. For $f\in L^2$, the truncated integrals $\int_{|x|\le R}f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx$ converge in $L^2$ to $\mathcal F_2f$ as $R\to\infty$. The corresponding positive-sign integrals converge in $L^2$ to $\mathcal F_2^{-1}f$. No pointwise convergence is asserted.

The map $\mathcal F:L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to BUC(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ is complex-linear and $\sup_\xi|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\|f\|_1$. Here $n\ge1$ and $BUC$ means bounded uniformly continuous functions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.

published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let

with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification

derivations.claim: Let $u$ lie in the left-hand kernel and take $u=z+\nabla q$ from [F1]. Then $\operatorname{curl}z=0$. By [F2], $z=\nabla r$ for $r\in H^1(\Omega)$. Since each $z_j\in H^1$, its weak derivatives give all second derivatives of $r$, so $r\in H^2(\Omega)$. Extend $r$ by [F3] to $a\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. This has a continuous representative: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|\widehat a\|_1\le\|(1+|\xi|^2)\widehat a\|_2\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1}\|_2<\infty$ in dimension three, and its positive-sign inverse integral $g(x)$ is the reflection of the integral Fourier transform of $\widehat a$, hence continuous by [F4]. Its truncated integrals converge uniformly to $g$, since the error is bounded by the $L^1$ Fourier tail, which tends to zero by dominated convergence. They converge in $L^2$ to $a$ by [F4]. On every finite-measure ball the uniform convergence is also $L^2$ convergence, so uniqueness of the $L^2$ limit there shows $g=a$ almost everywhere. Smooth compactly supported approximants to $a$ converge in $H^2$ by [F4] and uniformly by the same Fourier bound applied to their differences; no unproved $L^1$ inversion assumption on $a$ is made. Consequently $r$ has a continuous representative on $\overline\Omega$.

On any compact patch of the interior of a planar boundary face there is an inward rectangular slab of fixed height $b>0$ inside $\Omega$. For a smooth function on this slab, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem in the normal direction and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|f|_{s=0}\|_{L^2(\text{patch})}^2\le \frac{2}{b}\|f\|_{L^2(\text{slab})}^2+2b\|\partial_s f\|_{L^2(\text{slab})}^2.$ This defines a bounded $H^1$ face restriction by smooth approximation: the already proved Lipschitz extension [F3] on a bounded rectangular slab, followed by the whole-space density theorem [F4] at $k=1$, gives the required dense smooth restrictions. Since $z\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, approximating by compactly supported smooth vector fields shows that the restriction of $z$ to this patch is zero. Approximate $a$ from step 1.1 in $H^2$ by the smooth functions of [F4]; their gradients converge in $H^1$ on the slab and their values converge uniformly. Thus the restriction of $r$ is its continuous face value and the tangential derivatives of that restriction are the restrictions of the tangential components of $\nabla r=z$: integrate the smooth tangential derivative identity against a compactly supported smooth test on the face and pass to the limit using the slab estimate. These derivatives are zero. By [F3] in dimension two, the continuous boundary value of $r$ is constant on each connected planar face interior. One may split disconnected faces into their finitely many polygonal components. Continuity makes those constants extend to their closures. Since the boundary is connected by [F2] and these finitely many closed faces cover it, its continuous image under $r$ is a connected subset of a finite set of constants, hence one constant $c$.

Now $r-c\in H^1(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ vanishes on the boundary. By [F1] it lies in $H_0^1(\Omega)$. Thus $u=\nabla(q+r-c)$ belongs to the right-hand range. Its reverse inclusion follows directly from [F1], so the claimed relative kernel identity holds. This proves weak relative exactness using the actual boundary closure and continuum topology, rather than inferring it from mesh cohomology.

For the norm estimate, zero-extend $q\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ to $Q\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ by [F1], and fix a ball $B\supset\overline\Omega$ with $A=B\setminus\overline\Omega$ of positive measure. Ball Poincare in [F3] gives $\|Q-Q_B\|_{L^2(B)}\le C_B\|\nabla q\|_2$. Since $Q=0$ on $A$, $|Q_B||A|^{1/2}\le\|Q-Q_B\|_{L^2(B)}$. The triangle inequality therefore gives $\|q\|_2\le C_B(1+(|B|/|A|)^{1/2})\|\nabla q\|_2$, proving the asserted $H^1$ bound. If a sequence of gradients is Cauchy in $L^2$, this estimate makes its scalar representatives Cauchy in $H^1$. The space $H_0^1$ is closed by its definition as a closure, and complete as a closed subspace of $H^1$. Its limit's gradient is the given $L^2$ limit, so the gradient range is closed.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron with a matching shape-regular affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T_h$. There are a positive continuous piecewise affine function $g_h$, a smooth bounded vector field $b$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and positive constants $c,C,r,\epsilon_0$, independent of the mesh, with the following properties. On $K$, $c h_K\le g_h\le C h_K$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(g_h)\le C$, where $h_K=\operatorname{diam}K$. Put
$$F_{t,y}^{\pm}(x)=x+t g_h(x)(\pm b(x)+r y),\qquad |y|\le1,\quad 0<t\le\epsilon_0.$$
The maps are uniformly bi-Lipschitz on their domain. For the plus sign, $F_{t,y}^{+}(\overline\Omega)\subset\Omega$. For the minus sign, $F_{t,y}^{-}(\partial\Omega)\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline\Omega$, at distance at least $ctg_h(x)$ from $\partial\Omega$. The same interior distance lower bound holds for the plus sign at boundary points. The images of $K$ and all homotopies $s\mapsto F_{st,y}^{\pm}(x)$, $x\in K$, lie within distance $Ct h_K$ of $K$. Their intersections with $\Omega$ are contained in a vertex patch $\omega_K$ of uniformly bounded overlap, after decreasing $\epsilon_0$ if necessary. All constants may depend on $\Omega$ and the shape-regularity bound. No ratio of global maximum to minimum mesh size occurs.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh. The four face-normal fluxes are unisolvent on each $RT_0(K)$, and matching face fluxes assemble a global $H(\operatorname{div})$ field. For smooth scalar $f$, smooth vector fields $u,v$, and the canonical interpolants determined by vertex values, oriented edge circulations, oriented face-normal fluxes, and cell integrals, the interpolation maps satisfy cellwise
$$
abla I_h^0f=I_h^1
abla f,\qquad \operatorname{curl}I_h^1u=I_h^2\operatorname{curl}u,\qquad \operatorname{div}I_h^2v=I_h^3\operatorname{div}v.$$
Any assignment of one real oriented value to each global mesh edge determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^1$; any assignment of one real oriented flux to each global mesh face determines a unique assembled field in $N_h^2$. These assemblies belong to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$, respectively, with the global spaces and conventions of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Applying the local moment identities to polynomial cell restrictions also proves that the global finite-element spaces form the subcomplex $W_h^0\xrightarrow{
abla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$. The canonical interpolation identities themselves apply to smooth inputs; they do not extend the canonical edge moments to arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ inputs.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
For every smooth map $F:M\to N$ and every form $\omega$ on $N$, $$d(F^*\omega)=F^*(d\omega).$$

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. The inverse estimate follows the same way for polynomial coefficients and their first derivatives. These arguments apply to degrees zero through three, taking $d=0$ in top degree.

We first justify all boundary and weak-differential operations used below. Using the smooth field $b$ from [F1], replace $g_h$ temporarily by the constant one and let $S_t^+$ be the average pullback by $x\mapsto x+t(b(x)+ry)$. Its image on $\overline\Omega$ has interior clearance $ct$. In coordinates the pullback coefficients are the minors displayed above, with $D_xF=I+tDb(x)$. The change of variables $z=x+t(b(x)+ry)$ writes this operator as integration against a smooth kernel in $x,z$, including the smooth pullback coefficients; hence it maps $L^2$ forms to forms smooth on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. More explicitly, with $\psi_t(x)=x+tb(x)$ it is the pullback $\psi_t^*(\check\rho_{tr}*\widetilde u)$, where $\check\rho(y)=\rho(-y)$ and $\widetilde u$ is zero extension of the coefficient vector: the pullback minors are independent of $y$. This also proves independence of representatives and absolute integrability. Reconstruction and step 1.1 give the first claimed bound after summing the bounded-overlap patches. At boundary simplices the outward images lie strictly outside $\overline\Omega$, so every minus moment there vanishes.

For a piecewise Whitney form with all boundary tangential moments zero, zero extension has distributional $d$ equal to its piecewise $d$, extended by zero. Indeed integrate cellwise against a compact test form: the interior-face terms cancel by matching tangential traces [F2], and boundary terms vanish because zero boundary moments give zero entire tangential polynomial trace. Use $S_t^-$, defined as in step 1.2 with $-b$, on that zero extension. It is smooth and zero on a collar of the boundary, since every outward sample from sufficiently near the boundary lies outside $\overline\Omega$. There is also a boundary-corrected family of projections $\pi_{h,0}^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_{h,0}^k$, where $E_{h,0}^k=E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ and $H_0\Lambda^k$ is the graph closure of compactly supported smooth forms. These have the same uniform bounds, are the identity on $E_{h,0}^k$, and commute on the homogeneous complex. In particular,
$$\pi_{h,0}^0:H_0^1(\Omega)\to W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega),\qquad \pi_{h,0}^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega),\qquad \nabla\pi_{h,0}^0=\pi_{h,0}^1\nabla.$$

Each family converges strongly in $L^2$ on every $L^2$ form, uniformly on compact $L^2$ subsets, and in the graph norm on its corresponding graph domain. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Put $B=\nabla H_0^1$, closed by [F5]. For a graph-bounded sequence $v_h\in X_h$, choose the decompositions $v_h=z_h+\nabla q_h$ from [F2], using AC on this countable family of nonempty decomposition sets. The sequence $z_h$ is bounded in $H_0^1$. By [F4], extract a subsequence on which all three components converge in $L^2$, using three successive subsequences. On this subsequence the lifts $w_h=(I-P_B)v_h=(I-P_B)z_h$ converge in $L^2$, since $I-P_B$ is a contraction.

The continuous kernel $K$ is closed in $L^2$: if $k_j\in K$ converges in $L^2$, it is Cauchy in the curl graph norm, its graph limit lies in $H_0(\operatorname{curl})$ by the closure definition, and its curl remains zero. Let $P_K$ be its orthogonal projection. A graph-bounded sequence $u_j\in Y:=H_0(\operatorname{curl})\cap K^\perp$ satisfies $u_j=(I-P_K)z_j$ by [F2], since $\nabla q_j\in K$. Therefore the same componentwise Rellich argument proves compactness of $Y\hookrightarrow L^2$. If no continuous curl Poincare constant existed on $Y$, choose $u_j\in Y$ with $\|u_j\|_2=1$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}u_j\|_2<1/j$. Compactness gives $u_j\to u$ in $L^2$ along a subsequence; their curls tend to zero, so graph closure puts $u\in K$, while the closed orthogonality conditions put $u\in K^\perp$ and $\|u\|_2=1$. This contradiction proves $\|u\|_2\le C_\Omega\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2$ on $Y$.

The gap estimate [F5], using the relative degree-zero commutation in [F1], gives $\|v_h-w_h\|_2\le\|\Pi_h^1w_h-w_h\|_2\to0$. For clarity, this last limit uses both strong convergence on each fixed field and the uniform $L^2$ operator bound; it does not follow from pointwise convergence alone on a moving sequence. The strong limit of $w_h$ need only lie in $L^2$: the bounded extensions converge on all $L^2$ by density, as proved in [F5]. Hence $v_h$ converges strongly along the same subsequence. This proves discrete compactness without any topological exactness assumption.

For $v_h\in Z_h$, set $w=(I-P_K)v_h\in Y$. Its curl equals that of $v_h$. This curl belongs to the next relative graph space: approximate $v_h$ by compactly supported smooth fields in the curl graph norm; their curls converge in $L^2$, have zero divergence, and are compactly supported, hence converge also in the divergence graph norm. Since the finite element spaces form the relative subcomplex, $\operatorname{curl}v_h$ belongs to its discrete degree-two target. Commutation and identity on that discrete next-degree space therefore imply $e=v_h-\Pi_h^1w\in K_h$. Hence $(v_h,e)=0$, and $\|v_h\|_2^2=(v_h,\Pi_h^1w)\le M\|v_h\|_2\|w\|_2\le MC_\Omega\|v_h\|_2\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_2$. Division when $v_h\ne0$ proves the mesh-uniform inequality on $Z_h$; the zero case is immediate. No limit in $h$ or finite-coarse-mesh exception is required for this inequality.

On the original contractible domain, [F3] implies $K_h=V_h\cap B$. If $v_h=\nabla p\in K_h$ with $p\in H_0^1$, then on every tetrahedron $v_h=a+b\times x$ has curl $2b=0$, so it is constant and $p$ is affine there. The piecewise affine representatives have matching traces on each shared face because they represent one $H^1$ function; equality almost everywhere of two affine face polynomials is equality everywhere on that face, including its vertices. At each mesh vertex the incident tetrahedra are connected through shared faces containing that vertex: the link is a triangulated sphere at an interior vertex and a triangulated disk at a boundary vertex, since the matching mesh realizes the Lipschitz three-manifold with boundary. A path in this link, perturbed to miss its finitely many vertices, gives the required face chain. Equality of the affine values therefore propagates to every tetrahedron incident at the vertex. The common nodal values assemble a continuous piecewise affine function on $\overline\Omega$, equal to $p$ almost everywhere, hence in $W_h^0$. Its trace on every open boundary triangle is zero since $p\in H_0^1$; the affine trace polynomial is consequently zero everywhere on that triangle. Every boundary vertex belongs to such a triangle, so all boundary nodal values vanish and the assembled function belongs to $S_h$. Conversely $\nabla S_h\subset K_h$. Consequently $K_h=B_h$, $Z_h=X_h$, and step 2.2 is the asserted inequality on $X_h$.

In general topology $B\subset K$ and $B_h\subset K_h$. Closedness of $B$ gives $K=B\oplus\mathcal H$, while finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition gives $K_h=B_h\oplus\mathcal H_h$ and $Z_h=X_h\cap\mathcal H_h^\perp$. The unit ball of $\mathcal H$ is graph bounded and lies in $B^\perp$; [F2] and [F4] make it relatively compact by the argument in step 1.1. A Hilbert space with compact unit ball is finite dimensional: otherwise choose successive unit vectors orthogonal to their predecessors, obtaining pairwise distance $\sqrt2$ and contradicting compactness. The discrete harmonic space is finite dimensional as a subspace of $V_h$. Nonzero $a_h\in\mathcal H_h$ has $\|a_h\|_2>0$ but curl zero, disproving a curl Poincare bound on all $X_h$ whenever such a mode exists. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 still prove compactness of $X_h$ and step 2.2 proves the quotient inequality. The proof uses AC for selections and imported analytic suppliers, CC for the projection/Poincare interfaces, and CC/DC through the exact Rellich supplier; it asserts no choice-free version.
